name: Upadacitinib (alopecia)

card.summary: An oral JAK1 inhibitor approved for several inflammatory diseases and studied for alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss.
card.note: Prescription immunosuppressant with a boxed warning; not for pattern baldness.

quick.overview:
Upadacitinib (brand name Rinvoq) is a once-daily oral JAK1 inhibitor from AbbVie. It is approved for conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, atopic dermatitis and Crohn's disease, and has been examined for alopecia areata, where the immune system attacks hair follicles.

For people with alopecia areata, the appearance goal is regrowth of scalp, brow or beard hair. A 2025 review in Skin Appendage Disorders covers the evidence for upadacitinib in alopecia. Related JAK inhibitors have phase 3 data in the condition.
quick.how: It is a prescription tablet managed by physicians. Looksmaxxing forum posts mention alopecia areata mostly as an autoimmune problem distinct from male pattern baldness.
quick.risks: The FDA requires a boxed warning for upadacitinib covering serious infections, heart events, cancer, blood clots and death. Common effects include upper respiratory infections, nausea, cough and fever.

lead: Upadacitinib, sold as Rinvoq, is a selective Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) inhibitor taken by mouth. It blocks JAK-STAT signalling, which relays inflammatory cytokine signals.[2][9] It was approved in the US in August 2019 for rheumatoid arthritis, with later indications including atopic dermatitis, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.[2]

For hair, it is of interest in alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which immune cells attack hair follicles and hair falls out in patches; regrowth of scalp, eyebrow and eyelash hair is the appearance payoff.[8] In July and August 2025 AbbVie announced positive topline results from its two replicate phase 3 UP-AA studies in severe alopecia areata.[10][11] A 2025 review, "Upadacitinib for Alopecia: Current Evidence and Clinical Insights," summarises the research.[3]

Other JAK inhibitors are already approved for severe alopecia areata: baricitinib (2022), ritlecitinib (2023) and deuruxolitinib (2024), the last of which reported a phase 3 trial (THRIVE-AA1).[4][8] Upadacitinib itself is not approved for alopecia areata, and it is not a treatment for androgenetic alopecia (male pattern baldness).[10]

chain: Hair regrowth on scalp, brows and lashes
angle.text: In alopecia areata the immune system targets follicles; JAK inhibitors are studied to calm that response so hair can regrow. In the phase 3 UP-AA trials, regrowth was measured as scalp coverage plus eyebrow and eyelash improvement. It is not a treatment for androgenetic alopecia.

sections.h: Alopecia areata and the appearance goal
paras: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks normally protected hair follicles, producing coin-sized bald patches on the scalp and sometimes loss of beard, brow, lash or body hair. In rare cases it progresses to loss of all scalp or body hair.[8] Roughly 2 percent of people are affected at some point in life, and onset is often in childhood or young adulthood.[8]

Hair often regrows on its own in limited cases, but relapses are common, and recovery is less likely when all body hair is lost.[8] Because visible hair loss can affect self-image and is associated with anxiety and social difficulty, regrowth on the scalp, brows and lashes is the main goal of treatment.[8] JAK inhibitors are the newest class of systemic treatment: baricitinib, ritlecitinib and deuruxolitinib have each been approved by the FDA for severe disease.[8]

Approved uses include rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, axial spondyloarthritis, atopic dermatitis, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.[2] Alopecia areata use is investigational and confined to clinical trials.[3][10]

Many cytokines signal through receptors that depend on Janus kinase enzymes, which activate STAT transcription factors; blocking JAKs dampens that signalling.[9] Upadacitinib is selective for JAK1, roughly 74-fold over JAK2 and 58-fold over JAK3, a selectivity that developers pursued because earlier, less selective JAK inhibitors had dose-limiting side effects.[2] The rationale in alopecia areata is that interferon-gamma and related cytokines drive the immune attack on follicles, and that interrupting them allows follicles to resume hair growth.[3]

Upadacitinib has phase 3 trials in atopic dermatitis, Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis and giant-cell arteritis.[5][6][7] In atopic dermatitis a head-to-head phase 3b trial compared it with dupilumab, and network meta-analyses have placed high-dose upadacitinib among the most effective systemic treatments for that condition.[12][13]

For alopecia areata, AbbVie's UP-AA programme consists of two replicate randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 studies in people aged 12 to 64 with severe disease, comparing two once-daily dose levels with placebo over a 24-week first period.[10][11] In Study 2 (announced 30 July 2025, mean baseline SALT score 83.8), 44.6 percent and 54.3 percent of participants on the lower and higher dose reached at least 80 percent scalp coverage (SALT 20 or less) at week 24, versus 3.4 percent on placebo.[10] In Study 1 (announced 21 August 2025, mean baseline SALT 84.0), the figures were 45.2 percent and 55.0 percent versus 1.5 percent on placebo.[11] Rates of at least 90 percent scalp coverage were 36.0 and 47.1 percent in Study 2 and 35.2 and 45.8 percent in Study 1, against 1.4 and 0.7 percent on placebo.[10][11] Both studies also met secondary endpoints for complete scalp coverage and eyebrow and eyelash improvement.[10][11]

These results come from company press releases of topline data rather than peer-reviewed papers. AbbVie stated that upadacitinib is not approved for alopecia areata and that regulators have not evaluated it for this use.[10][11] A 2025 review in Skin Appendage Disorders gathers earlier evidence on upadacitinib in alopecia.[3] The related JAK inhibitor deuruxolitinib was tested in the phase 3 THRIVE-AA1 randomized trial in adults with alopecia areata.[4]

Common effects include upper respiratory infections, nausea, cough and fever. The FDA boxed warning for upadacitinib, tofacitinib and baricitinib covers serious heart-related events, cancer, blood clots and death. The drug is contraindicated in active tuberculosis, severe infections, severe liver impairment and pregnancy.[2][9] The European Medicines Agency has recommended that several JAK inhibitors be used only when no suitable alternative exists in people aged 65 or older, those at high cardiovascular or cancer risk, and current or long-term former smokers; shingles risk is also raised.[9]

In the UP-AA studies, AbbVie reported no new safety signals relative to approved indications. The most common events were upper respiratory tract infection, acne, nasopharyngitis and raised creatine phosphokinase; serious adverse events occurred in about 1.4 to 2.8 percent of treated participants, and discontinuations for adverse events in about 0.7 to 1.5 percent.[10][11] One venous thromboembolism (in a participant with multiple risk factors) was reported in Study 2, and one breast cancer case in Study 1.[10][11]

Forum threads discuss alopecia areata as an autoimmune condition separate from male pattern baldness, and one poster noted that pattern-baldness advice does not apply to people with the autoimmune form.[7] Discussion of upadacitinib specifically for hair is limited; most hair-loss threads concern finasteride, dutasteride and minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia.[14]

timeline.event: US approval for rheumatoid arthritis (August); EU approval in December.[2]
FDA approves upadacitinib for atopic dermatitis (January) and ulcerative colitis (March); baricitinib becomes the first JAK inhibitor approved for severe alopecia areata (June).[2][8]
Crohn's disease approvals in the UK, EU and US; ritlecitinib approved for alopecia areata (June).[2][8]
Deuruxolitinib approved for severe alopecia areata (July).[8]
AbbVie announces positive topline results from both phase 3 UP-AA studies (30 July and 21 August).[10][11]

lore.intro: Alopecia areata appears occasionally on looksmax.org, usually as a separate autoimmune issue from male pattern baldness.[7]

claims.claim: Autoimmune alopecia needs a different approach than male pattern baldness
claims.believers: A poster notes that pattern-baldness advice does not apply to those with an autoimmune disorder.[7]
claims.experts: Alopecia areata is immune-mediated and is the focus of JAK inhibitor trials, while androgenetic alopecia is hormone-mediated and treated with different drugs.[4][8]

claims.claim: JAK inhibitors can regrow hair in alopecia areata
claims.believers: Patients and advocates point to the newly approved JAK inhibitors as the first systemic treatments to restore substantial scalp hair.[8]
claims.experts: Phase 3 trials of deuruxolitinib and AbbVie's topline UP-AA results for upadacitinib report substantially more scalp regrowth than placebo over 24 weeks.[4][10][11]

claims.claim: Upadacitinib is a hair-loss option for men with pattern baldness
claims.believers: Some posts treat any hair-restoring drug as relevant to all hair loss.[14]
claims.experts: Upadacitinib's alopecia work concerns alopecia areata; its approved uses and trials do not include androgenetic alopecia, and it carries a boxed warning.[2][10]
